hero.title: Cushion Cut Diamond Guide: How to Choose the Right Shape, Ratio and Quality
hero.subheading: Compare square and elongated cushions by outline, ratio, facet pattern, spread, colour, clarity and setting—then inspect the actual stone, because the report alone cannot grade cushion cut quality.

paragraphs: A cushion cut diamond combines a square or rectangular outline with curved sides and softened corners. Its pillow-like shape can produce anything from broad, defined flashes to a finer crushed-ice appearance.
That variety is one of the cushion cut’s main attractions—but it also makes cushion diamonds harder to compare.

Two cushion cut natural diamonds can have the same carat, colour and clarity grades while displaying different outlines, face-up sizes, facet patterns and light performance. One may appear bright and balanced; another may hide weight below the girdle or show a dull centre.
Choosing well therefore requires more than finding an acceptable ratio or reading the laboratory report.

quickAnswer.title: Quick Answer
quickAnswer.question: A high-quality cushion cut diamond should have:
attributes: An attractive square or elongated outline
Good face-up size for its carat weight
A facet pattern that suits the buyer’s preference
No large persistent dark or watery areas
A secure girdle without vulnerable extremes
A price that reflects its complete visual quality
closingParagraphs: GIA reports may describe a diamond as Cushion Brilliant or Cushion Modified Brilliant, but GIA does not currently assign an overall cut grade to cushion diamonds.
The report should be used as a technical filter. The final decision must include inspection of the actual diamond or a reliable high-quality video.

keyTakeaways.title: Key Takeaways
items: Cushion cut diamonds can be square, rectangular or distinctly elongated.
There is no single ideal cushion cut ratio.
Ratio describes the outline but does not measure sparkle or cut quality.
GIA currently does not provide an overall cut grade for cushion diamonds.
Cushion Brilliant and Cushion Modified Brilliant are laboratory descriptions of facet arrangements.
“Crushed ice” is a trade description, not a standard GIA quality grade.
Modified brilliant does not automatically mean crushed ice.
Cushion diamonds can display broad flashes, fragmented reflections or a mixture of both.
Table and depth percentages should be used for comparison, not as universal pass-or-fail rules.
Carat measures weight, not visible size.
Compare millimetre measurements when judging face-up spread.
Rounded corners make cushions less vulnerable than shapes with sharp points, but the setting must still protect the stone.
Colour can appear differently depending on the facet pattern, metal and lighting.
Many cushion diamonds can be eye-clean at VS2 or carefully selected SI1, but every stone must be inspected.
The best cushion is the one that balances outline, brightness, spread, durability, documentation and price.

items.question: What is a cushion cut diamond?
items.answer: A cushion cut diamond has a square or rectangular outline with curved sides and rounded or softened corners. It uses brilliant-style facets and can display broad flashes, crushed-ice scintillation or a combination of both.

items.question: Is a square or elongated cushion cut better?
items.answer: Neither is universally better. Square cushions offer a balanced traditional appearance, while elongated cushions provide a longer silhouette. The choice should depend on outline preference, light performance, spread and setting design.

items.question: What is the best ratio for a cushion cut diamond?
items.answer: There is no universal best ratio. Ratios around 1.00–1.05 generally appear square, while ratios of approximately 1.16–1.30 appear elongated. These are comparison ranges, not quality grades.

items.question: Does GIA give cushion cut diamonds an overall cut grade?
items.answer: No. GIA currently assigns an overall cut grade only to standard round brilliant diamonds in the D-to-Z colour range. Cushion reports may still include polish, symmetry, table, depth and other technical information.

items.question: What is the difference between Cushion Brilliant and Cushion Modified Brilliant?
items.answer: The terms describe different facet arrangements. Cushion brilliants often show broader, more defined reflections, while modified brilliants may show smaller or more fragmented reflections. The actual diamond must be inspected because the report description does not guarantee its appearance.

items.question: Is a crushed-ice cushion diamond bad?
items.answer: No. Crushed ice is a visual style, not a quality grade. It can be attractive when the diamond remains bright and lively. Avoid stones that appear watery, grey, mushy or inactive through the centre.

items.question: What colour and clarity are best for a cushion cut?
items.answer: G–H colour with VS2 clarity is a strong general starting range. A carefully selected SI1 may provide better value when it is eye-clean and transparent. The ideal combination depends on the diamond, setting and budget.

items.question: Do cushion cut diamonds look larger than round diamonds?
items.answer: Not always. Some cushions carry more weight in their depth and may appear smaller than expected. Compare length and width measurements rather than relying on carat weight alone.

items.question: Is a cushion cut better than a radiant cut?
items.answer: Neither is automatically better. Cushions have curved sides and a softer outline, while radiants have straighter sides and cropped corners. Compare brightness, spread, outline and facet pattern before deciding.

items.question: What setting is best for a cushion cut diamond?
items.answer: Solitaire, halo, bezel, pavé and three-stone settings can all work well. The best setting depends on the cushion’s outline, dimensions, girdle condition and the buyer’s preferred style.

finalTakeaway.title: Choose the Cushion That Performs—Not Just the Ratio on Paper
introParagraphs: Cushion cut quality is judged through outline, facet pattern, spread, brightness, durability and documentation—not a single ratio or laboratory label.
Decide square or elongated, inspect videos carefully, and approve the stone that looks and performs correctly for its intended jewellery.
